html:
Pearl diving was the main business of Bahrain for centuries and peaked in the 1800s and early 1900s, when the island was the chief pearl market of the Gulf.

Each summer hundreds of boats left Muharraq for the oyster beds. Divers went down on a rope with a stone weight and a nose clip, again and again through the day. Most were bound to their captains by debts that passed from father to son. Merchants sold the pearls on to Bombay and from there to Europe.

The trade collapsed in the 1930s, hit by the Great Depression and by cheap cultured pearls from Japan, made by the method of Kokichi Mikimoto. Oil arrived at the same moment. Merchant houses, oyster beds and a seashore of Muharraq are now a World Heritage Site. See also pearl hunting.
sum: Pearl diving was the main business of Bahrain for centuries and peaked in the 1800s and early 1900s, when the island was the chief pearl market of the Gulf.
